text: So the most basic motivation for sorting comes from searching.
As we have seen, if you have an unsorted array, you have to search for it by scanning the entire array from beginning to end.
So you spend linear time searching for the element.
Whereas if you had the sorted array, you can probe it at the midpoint and use binary search and achieve the same result in logarithmic time.
And logarithmic time is considerably faster than linear time.
Now there are other advantages to having the elements sorted.
For instance, if you want to find the median, the value for which half the elements are bigger and half the elements are smaller.
Well, the median in a sorted array is clearly the midpoint of the array.
If you want to do some other kind of statistical things such as building a frequency table of values, when you sort these values, they all come together.
So all the equal values will be in a contiguous block.
So it's much easier to find how many copies of each value are there.
And in particular, if you want only one copy of every value, if you want to remove all duplicates from the array, then you can scan the sorted array from beginning to end.
And for each block of values, keep just one copy.
So there are very many different reasons why one might want to sort an array to make further computation on the array much easier.
So let's imagine how we would like to sort an array.
So forget about arrays and think about just sorting something which is given to you as a physical collection of objects.
So say you are a teaching assistant for a course and the instructor, the teacher who is teaching the course, has corrected the exams and now wants you to sort the exam papers in order of marks.
So say your task is to arrange them in descending order.
How would you go about this task?
So one naive strategy is the following.
You would go through the entire stack and keep track of the smallest mark that you have seen.
At the end of your pass, you have the paper in your hand which has the smallest mark among the marks allotted to all the students.
So you move this to a new pile. Then you repeat the process.
So go through the remaining papers after having discarded the smallest one into a new pile and look for the next smallest one.
Move that on top of the new pile and so on.
So after the second pass, you have the second smallest mark on the pile, after the third pass, you have the third smallest mark on the pile.
And as you can imagine, after n passes, you have moved all n papers from the whole pile to the new pile in descending order.
So this particular strategy can be illustrated as follows.
So supposing we have this list or array of six elements.
So in the first pass, we look for the smallest value.
So the smallest value in this case is 21.
So we moved 21 to a new list and removed from the original list.
Now we repeat the scan.
Among the remaining values, the value 32 is the smallest one.
So we remove that and move it to the new list.
We keep doing this. So at the next step, we move 55 and then we move 64 and then we move 74 and then we move 89.
So in this process, if this had been a vertical stack, 21 would be at the bottom, 89 would be at the top.
And so we would have the list sorted from top to bottom and descending order.
In this case, it is from right to left and descending order or from left to right and ascending order.
So this strategy is called selection sort.
So we select in each round the next element, which is the smallest and therefore the next to be put out in the sorted order.
And move it to its correct position, that is to the end of the final sorted list.
Now this version of selection sort that we just described builds a second list.
In other words, in order to sort one pile, we have to create a second pile of papers.
Now we can easily eliminate the second pile of papers if we do the following.
When we find the minimum element, we know it must go to the beginning of the list.
So instead of creating a new list, we move it to the beginning of the current list.
Of course, in the beginning of the current list, there is another value.
So we have to do something with that value.
So we just exchange the positions.
So we find the minimum position and swap the value at that minimum position with the value at the first position.
Now the smallest value in the entire array has moved to the beginning.
So now we start from the second element onwards and look for the minimum again.
This will be the second smallest.
So we now having found that we will move that to the second position in the array.
So we keep doing this and without using a second list, we are able to do the same sorting that we did before.
So to see how this works, we take the same array that we had before.
As we said, in the first round, we identify 21 as the minimum element, which is marked in red.
And the first position is 74.
So we would like 21 to be at the beginning of this list.
So since 74 is there, we exchange 21 and 74 and we get this new list.
In this new list, now 21 is marked in green to indicate that it is in its final position.
It is the smallest value.
It has moved to where it should be in the sorted list.
So now we scan the remaining elements and we identify the 32 is the smallest element.
Now 32 already happens to be in the second position.
So we could think of exchanging it with itself or doing nothing depending on how we want to interpret it.
So 32 now becomes marked green so that it stays in the correct position.
Now in the remaining list, 55 is the smallest element marked in red.
But it has to be at position 3, which is occupied by 89 marked in yellow.
So we exchange these two and now we have 55 and third position.
So we keep doing this.
So at the next step, we will identify 64 and swap it into the fourth position.
And then we find that 74 is already in the correct position.
So we leave it where it is.
And finally, of course, 89 is the only element.
So when you have a list of one element, there is no sorting to be done.
So this procedure can be described by a very simple iterative algorithm.
So what we do is that we have, if you remember, we start by scanning the entire array.
That is from 0 to n minus 1.
We look for the minimum element in that segment.
So we have a iteration which basically starts at the starting position.
And then from the starting position onwards, it assumes that the beginning is the minimum value.
And whenever you find a smaller value, you mark that as a minimum position.
Now having done all this, you have now found the minimum from a 0 to a n minus 1.
Then you move this value to the beginning.
So you swap the starting position and the minimum position.
Now we have the smallest value at a 0.
So now you go back to this loop and now you move starting position from 0 to 1.
So you do the same scan for a 1 to a n minus 1.
And now the starting position is 1.
So at the end, you swap the second smallest element to a 1.
Then you do it for a 2 to a n minus 1 and so on.
So this is the simple iterative version of selection sort.
Where we just start with the entire array, move the smallest element to the first element, first position.
Then we take the rest of the array from a 1 onwards, move the smallest element to a 1.
Then start with a 2 and find the smallest element move it to a 2 and so on.
So how much time does this algorithm take?
So clearly in order to find the minimum element in an unsorted segment of length k,
we have to scan the entire segment and this takes k steps.
And each iteration, the segment to be scanned reduces by 1.
So we start by scanning all n elements, then we scan n minus 1 elements, then we scan n minus 2 elements and so on.
So we have overall the number of steps is n plus n minus 1 plus n minus 2 down to 1,
which is just the usual summation i is equal to 1 to n of i.
And this we know is n into n plus 1 by 2, which is order n squared.
So this naive algorithm selection sort in this iterative implementation is n squared.
Now there is another way of looking at selection sort.
So remember we said that we start by finding the minimum element moving it to the front and then doing the same thing.
Whenever you say do the same thing, it's useful to think of this as a recursive algorithm just to convince yourself that what you're doing is correct.
So in order to sort in general a from some position i to n minus 1,
what we do is we find the minimum value in the segment that is from a to i minus a i to a in minus 1 and move it to the beginning, which is a i.
So we have an array a and then we are at a position i and the last position in minus 1 and we are trying to sort this.
So what we are saying is we'll find the minimum somewhere and then exchange the value here.
And now what is now achieved by this is that this position is now correct.
So the value at a is now in the correct position and therefore we now need to sort from i plus 1 to n minus 1.
And how do we do this recursively? We just apply selection sort.
So we apply selection sort to a from i plus 1 to n minus 1 and this procedure stops when we have only one element.
So if you are going to start from a i is equal to n minus 1 to n minus 1, then we do nothing.
So this the reason to think of it recursively, one reason is that the code becomes a little easier to read.
So you say that you want to start sort a from start to n where start is the index of the unsorted segment where it begins and n is the total size.
So the last position is exactly n minus 1.
So if start is n minus 1 or bigger, then you do nothing, you just return.
Otherwise you find the smallest value in this segment from start to n minus 1.
So this is the same loop we did earlier.
We start with the minimum position being the beginning of this segment and then we keep walking forwards and whenever we find a value which is smaller than the minimum position we updated.
And at the end of this loop, we exchanged the position that we have found the value at that position with the starting position.
So now the correct value, so some value from say here has moved to the correct position.
And now we recursively sort a starting at position start plus 1 up to n.
So is this any different in complexity?
So let us write.
So remember when we did recursive calculations, we said that typically you would write a recurrence.
You would express the complexity of the algorithm itself in a recursive way.
So suppose tn is the number of steps you need to run selection sort and length n.
So the first thing is it requires n steps in order to find the minimum and move it to the beginning.
And then having moved it to the beginning, the rest of the array that is left to sort is up size n minus 1.
So you need time recursively tn minus 1.
So therefore you have tn. So this is the time to find the minimum.
Tn is n plus tn minus 1, which is the recursive step.
And we said that if we are sorting an array of size 1, we don't have to do anything, which is returns.
So t of 1 is 1.
So t of n is n plus tn minus 1.
But now if I take tn minus 1 and I expand it using the same expression, I get n minus 1 plus tn minus 2.
Now if I expand tn minus 2, I will get n minus 2 plus tn minus 3 and so on.
